label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
# Fourteen years of nights

Hello. It's been a while. I haven't posted since spring, and I've sat down to write this one several times since the weekend. Each time it has turned into either a eulogy or a complaint about the NHS. Nobody has died, and you've had plenty of the second from me already, so I'm going to try for neither.

On Saturday I worked my last ever night shift. 21:00 to 07:30, in majors. I'm not going to describe it, because the people in it aren't mine to write about. I'll only say that I had half expected the shift to know it was the last one and behave accordingly. It didn't.

My first night was in 2012, as an SHO, which makes it fourteen years. Since Monday I've been on the days-only rota. Some of that is my knees and my sleep. Some of it is my GP, who told me my blood pressure is not a joke anymore, in a voice I recognised because I use it on other people. I nodded in all the places my own patients nod.

I thought I'd be delighted. I am surprisingly not okay about it.

I drove home on Sunday morning down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up. Somewhere along there it landed that I will not see that light from this side again. I'll see plenty of sunrises. But I'll be driving in underneath them with the whole day still to do, and that isn't the same as driving home with the night behind you, slightly wrecked, while everybody else is only starting.

So I've been trying to work out, honestly, what nights gave me and what they took.

## What they took

Sleep, first of all. Anyone who has done nights knows you never quite pay it back, and my blood pressure seems to agree.

My first winter of nights, I sat in the car park at the Infirmary and cried because I couldn't remember whether I had given the second dose. I had. What has stayed with me is the frost on the windscreen, and the feeling of being handed a doubt at the exact moment I had nothing left to argue with it. That's a thing nights do.

They took time with my family too. My sister lives in Bangalore, and I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies. I was only ever going to be there on a screen, and both times nights meant I wasn't even that. My sister has never once complained about it. She reads this blog, so: I noticed. Thank you.

## What they gave

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers, and more honesty, and more kindness. At three in the morning nobody has the energy to perform. If someone asks whether you're all right, they want to know, and if you say you're not, somebody puts the kettle on.

People who haven't done them think nights are about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. Mostly they're about staying kind at 5am when you're empty, and then doing it again for the next person through the door. I learned that on nights, and I'm not sure I would have learned it anywhere else.

I keep patients out of this blog, but I'll allow myself one, with nothing in it that could tell you who he was. An elderly gentleman, in the small hours, held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. He went home a few days later. That's all I'm going to say about him, but I've thought about it a lot this week.

And there's the toast. Someone always makes toast in the staff room at 4am. In fourteen years, nobody has ever admitted to starting it. You notice the smell and you follow it. I have my suspicions, and I'm not going to name them here because several of them read this.

## The bit I've been avoiding

I'm relieved. I'm relieved, and I feel like a traitor for being relieved.

This isn't a staffing post. I've written enough of those. It's simpler than that. The people I did those nights with are still doing them, and I've got off. I can't even blame age. Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has done them for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. Every time.

I don't have a tidy way to settle it. I needed to stop, and I'm going to miss it, and I've given up trying to make those two agree.

So I'll finish with the toast and leave myself out of it. If you're on nights this winter and you find yourself in that staff room at four, have a slice. Don't ask who started it. And don't try to race Folasade up the stairs.

---

This comes to about 800 words, the bottom of your range. Four things to check before you post:

- **The patient:** I dropped "last winter" and "3am" and changed "three days" to "a few days", so no one could place him.
- **The naming ceremonies:** I assumed you were meant to join by video and nights stopped even that. Change the line if you did watch on a screen.
- **Folasade:** I avoided pronouns because I didn't want to guess.
- **My additions:** The kettle, the GP's voice and your "suspicions" about the toast are mine, so cut any that aren't true.
